transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-09 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~58m
Attendees: Sofia Martin (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Riley Park (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (NexaHealth ML), Marcus Green (NexaHealth Platform), Elena Ruiz (NexaHealth CTO), Jonas Weber (NexaHealth SRE)
Summary (auto): Weekly POC checkpoint focused on throughput tuning. SE presented last week's perf runs, discussed continuous batching behavior and queue depth settings. Action items agreed for synthetic rerun and pricing update.
00:00:05 Sofia: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick roll call. we've got 60 minutes, main focus is the throughput numbers from the pilot this week and tuning next steps.
00:00:22 Priya: thanks, yes excited to see the retune results — last week we saw some weird tail latency spikes around midday traffic.
00:00:35 Daniel: quick context — we ran the cont-batch patch two days ago, enabled adaptive batching and lowered the max queue depth from 256 to 128 for the service lane that routes to the h100 pool. baseline was A100 previously.
00:00:54 Marcus: one clarification: when you say queue depth is 128, that's per GPU queue, right? not per-instance?
00:01:05 Daniel: correct, per-GPU queue depth (we treated each slot as a GPU worker). we also constrained per-instance concurrency to 12 to avoid context-switch thrashing.
00:01:22 Elena: and the model variant is the 8-bit quantized v2 we pinned for the pilot?
00:01:30 Riley: yes, q8_0-v2 with shallow kvcache warmup. though the transcription on some logs shows 'K V cache' spelled weirdly, ignore the auto parsing.
00:02:10 Sofia: can you walk us through the main metric deltas from the last run? throughput, p50/p95, and any big error classes?
00:02:25 Daniel: sure — quick numbers: prior to changes we were avg 320 qps sustained on the dedicated pool, after continuous batching and queue depth tune we saw bursts to 700 qps with a sustained window at ~520 qps under the synthetic profile. p50 moved from 45ms to 38ms; p95 improved from 320ms down to 210ms in most buckets, but there are still intermittent 800ms spikes correlated with long prompts and cache misses.
00:03:05 Jonas: those 800ms spikes — are they correlated with KV cache evictions or a cold-start actor?
00:03:13 Daniel: mostly cache misses and the occasional fallback to smaller batch sizes when a long-sequence request lands. we saw queue-thrashing when concurrency hits 18 per instance; that's why we capped at 12.
00:03:40 Priya: we ran a few end-to-end tests with our front-end sim and observed request queuing around 300ms occasionally — impacting perceived latency. we're trying to balance user visible latency vs throughput.
00:04:00 Marcus: question on batching behavior — does continuous batching add head-of-line blocking if a long prompt sits at the front?
00:04:10 Riley: good question — continuous batching in Redwood defers batching cutoff based on a small timer and token arrival; a very long prompt can indeed delay a small prompt behind it if they target the same batch window, but the runtime implements dynamic batch shuffling heuristics to mitigate HVLB. in practice we saw a few cases.
00:04:50 Elena: were you able to test the routing fallback? if H100 pool saturates will it fallback to A100 or a lower-cost instance?
00:04:59 Daniel: yes, we configured smart routing for this pilot: primary route to H100 dedicated nodes, fallback to A100 dedicated nodes with a slightly different quantization profile. fallback incurred ~40ms extra overhead due to kernel mismatch.
00:05:20 Sofia: any observed QoE regressions when fallback happened?
00:05:25 Daniel: not for most prompts, but for some temperature-sensitive prompts we saw output divergence; PR for automated evals will catch those.
00:06:00 Priya: can you share the raw logs? we want to correlate with our client-side traces.
00:06:08 Daniel: yes i'll upload the perf traces to the pilot folder, the file names are perf-0108-h100-2hr.tar.gz etc. note the auto transcription sometimes mangles file names.
00:07:12 Sofia: walk us through the tuning knobs you changed this week — list and impact.
00:07:20 Daniel: changed knobs: reduced per-GPU queue depth 256->128, per-instance concurrency cap 18->12, enabled adaptive continuous batching with a 5ms commit timer (was 10ms), enabled prefix KV caching at 512-token window for sessioned flows, adjusted the batching-weight heuristic to favor shorter sequences. impact: higher sustained throughput, lower p95 on short requests, but exposes tail spikes on long-session cache misses.
00:08:05 Marcus: how stable was memory usage on the H100s? any OOMs?
00:08:12 Daniel: memory was stable, low-water mark stayed at 80% overall with spikes to 92% during heavy long-seq bursts. no OOMs in the run.
00:08:40 Priya: we saw a small increase in token cost due to more effective batching (more tokens per GPU call) but net cost per useful response went down. please include cost delta in the spreadsheet.
00:08:55 Sofia: noted, will include cost per 1k tokens and cost per 1k responses.
00:09:30 Jonas: question about backpressure — when queue depth is hit what happens upstream? do you return 429s or queue in a front-tier buffer?
00:09:42 Daniel: the current pilot uses a combination: short-term rate limiter on the edge returns 429 after a soft queue backlog threshold; Redwood runtime also supports polite queueing and graceful degradation policies. prototype uses polite queueing for high-priority routes.
00:10:05 Marcus: we want to avoid customer-facing 429s. prefer smoothing via front-tier buffer for 5s windows. can Redwood support that?
00:10:14 Riley: yes — we can bump the edge buffer and apply token-bucket smoothing for 5s bursts. tradeoff is increased client-side latency during smoothing.
00:11:02 Priya: what's your recommended concurrency target for our workload? we saw good numbers at 520 qps sustained with 12 concurrency per instance — can we bump to 16 to get 700+ sustained?
00:11:18 Daniel: safe ramp plan: test 14 then 16; we saw queue-thrashing at 18. also need to monitor kernel queuing time and PCIe contention.
00:11:40 Sofia: propose SE run the synthetic at 14 concurrency for 1 hour then 16 for 30 minutes and share traces.
00:11:52 Daniel: will do.
00:12:20 Elena: any impact expected on our request router (Envoy) or connection limits?
00:12:26 Marcus: we may need to tune envoy timeouts and upstream connection pool size. I'll coordinate with Jonas to open those limits during the test window.
00:12:40 Jonas: noted.
00:13:05 Priya: can we get a graph of batch size distribution over time? that's the metric we need to understand micro batching impact.
00:13:12 Daniel: yes — distribution graph included in the perf bundle; i'll make a simplified slide for the next call showing median and tail batch size.
00:13:45 Sofia: let's surface two specific experiments for this week: 1) concurrency ramp (14,16) synthetic; 2) increase queue depth to 192 but keep per-instance concurrency at 14 to see if backpressure shapes better.
00:14:00 Priya: why 192? earlier you cut from 256 to 128 and it helped — curious about the logic to go back up.
00:14:10 Daniel: the idea is to decouple per-GPU queue depth from per-instance concurrency to find a sweet spot where batching gains offset queue latency; sometimes slightly higher queue depth helps batching efficiency without hurting tail if concurrency is controlled.
00:15:00 Marcus: please log the exact routing decisions when fallback happens — we need the decision trace to align with our observability.
00:15:06 Riley: will include route decision trace IDs in the perf logs.
00:15:30 Sofia: open question — do you want to extend the pilot to include a Private deployment for one of your sensitive routes? NexaHealth still evaluating.
00:15:45 Elena: yes we'd like to try the Private control plane for the appointments route; need compliance checklist and network diagrams.
00:15:58 Sofia: we'll send the Private trial docs; AE action item to follow up.
00:16:30 Priya: small nit: some of the automated evals flagged hallucination regressions on fallback to A100 — is there a simple mitigation?
00:16:40 Daniel: mitigation path: add a scoring/regression filter that rejects outputs below a threshold; longer term, align quant profiles across pools or warm kernels.
00:17:10 Jonas: about the synthetic load: can we simulate a 60/40 mix of short & long prompts? that's our production mix.
00:17:20 Daniel: yes synthetic will mimic the 60/40 distribution and the token length histogram you shared.
00:18:00 Priya: timeline check — when can we expect the updated numbers?
00:18:05 Daniel: i'll run the ramp tests tomorrow (2026-01-10) and upload traces the following day.
00:18:12 Sofia: AE will send pricing by Monday (2026-01-11).
00:18:30 Priya: perfect.
00:19:00 — [fast-forward to mid-run results discussion, timestamps approximate] —
00:35:05 Daniel: mid-run note — we observed a pathological case where a particular prompt pattern causes batch queuing to hold for 12ms extra; correlates with client-side pre-processing that concatenates multiple short messages into one long payload.
00:36:10 Marcus: we can change the front-end to split messages earlier; we'll try that for the next test.
00:40:00 Priya: question about logs — we saw some requests tagged with error code E427 in your telemetry, can you decode?
00:40:12 Daniel: E427 is our internal queue-truncated code — essentially we aborted a batch because it exceeded the runtime safety window. it's configurable.
00:42:00 Sofia: any blockers to completing the next-step tests?
00:42:10 Elena: we need the compliance contacts and network diagrams to sign-off on Private trial but that is parallel.
00:43:00 Priya: one more ask — add a flag to synthetic runner to toggle 'prefer short-seq batching' to test different heuristics.
00:43:12 Daniel: will add that flag and include results.
00:44:30 Sofia: recap: SE will run concurrency ramp and queue-depth experiment, upload traces; AE to send pricing + private trial docs; NexaHealth to adjust Envoy and share prompt histogram. next meeting same time next week unless earlier needed.
00:45:05 Priya: yep thanks all.
00:45:20 Elena: thanks.
00:45:30 Sofia: closing — I'll post notes and action items in the pilot channel.
00:46:00 [call ends with casual sign-off]
